corpus_desc: 6 clips totalling 2 minutes 45 seconds, all from lossless CC licensed or public domain sources, plus two synthetic full band probes
vorbis_floor: refused every 32 kbps encode on this corpus outright
graph_a_note: The shape is the same in every test and has been since 2011. Opus first, AAC second, Vorbis and MP3 behind. In 2014 Opus scored 4.65 against Apple AAC at 4.40, with confidence intervals of ±0.07 and ±0.09, so the gap is real rather than noise. The MP3 in that test was given 136 kbps against Opus's 107 and still finished level with Vorbis. Note the 2006 row as well: at 128 kbps everything tied, including WMA Pro at 4.70 and LAME at 4.60. Above roughly 128 kbps the format argument stops mattering, which is why every test since has been run lower.
encoder_note: This is the single most useful pair of rows on the page. In the 2008 MP3 test every modern encoder was statistically tied, LAME 3.98.2 at 4.51, and the 1994 encoder l3enc, at the same 128 kbps and in the same format, scored 1.56: a gap of 2.95 grades that has nothing to do with MP3 and everything to do with the encoder. The 2011 AAC test says the same about AAC, 4.39 for Apple's encoder against 3.70 for Nero's, a spread of 0.69 grades at one bitrate in one format. MP3's bad reputation was earned by encoders, not by the standard.
voice_note: Averaged over the 5 tracks the 2014 test labels Voice, Opus scored 4.80, Apple AAC 4.57, LAME 4.34 at its higher bitrate, and Vorbis 4.01. Vorbis is last, and by a wider margin than on music: it lost 0.79 grades to Opus on speech against 0.41 over the whole set. This is the number that decides the podcast question, and it points at Opus, not at Vorbis.
bandwidth_note: At 64 kbps the four codecs made completely different decisions about what to keep: Opus held on to 20.5 kHz, Vorbis 15.4 kHz, AAC 12.1 kHz and MP3 11.4 kHz. At 32 kbps ffmpeg's AAC collapses to 3.8 kHz and MP3 to 5.9 kHz, which is the muffled telephone sound everyone recognises, while Opus is still coding to 20.3 kHz. Opus never lowpasses on this corpus: it sits at 20 kHz from 32 kbps to 320. AAC and MP3 only catch up above roughly 192 kbps.
achieved_note: Ask four encoders for 64 kbps and you get 71.6, 66.3, 64.2 and 55.2 kbps: a spread of 30% between the highest and the lowest. LAME in CBR hits its number exactly, every time. ffmpeg's AAC lands within a few percent. Opus in its default unconstrained VBR treats the number as a soft target and overshoots by 12% at 64 kbps, and its worst miss on this corpus was the spoken word clip, where a 64 kbps request produced 95 kbps. libvorbis in ABR mode runs the other way and undershoots by 14%. If you are filling a fixed pipe, this chart is the one that matters, and the answer is to measure rather than trust the flag.
lossless_note: Every lossless encode round tripped to identical PCM: 6 of 6 clips at FLAC level 8 and 6 of 6 for ALAC, checked as a SHA-256 over the decoded samples, not as a claim from the encoder. FLAC level 8 came out 54.1% under WAV and ALAC 49.4%, so FLAC is 9.4% smaller than ALAC on the same audio. The compression ladder flattens fast: going from level 0 to level 5 buys 7.3 percentage points, 5 to 8 buys 1.2 more, and 8 to 12 buys a further 0.8 for 5 times the encode time. Level 8 is the sensible stopping point.
speed_note: Nothing here is slow enough to matter for a file you encode once. Opus was the slowest encoder at 34 times realtime and MP3 the fastest at 55, both measured at 128 kbps on one thread. Decoding is another order of magnitude up and is where battery life actually lives: FLAC decoded at 565 times realtime, AAC at 397 and Opus at 251, the slowest of the set. On a phone that difference is real but small; on a battery powered embedded player it is one of the reasons AAC hardware decoders exist.
disagree_bandwidth: On the measured side Vorbis looks better than AAC at low bitrate: at 64 kbps it kept 15.4 kHz against AAC's 12.1 kHz, and at 48 kbps 14.3 kHz against 7.5 kHz. Listeners disagreed twice. In 2007 at 64 kbps, HE-AAC scored 3.74 and Vorbis 3.32; in 2011, Apple HE-AAC 3.82 against Vorbis 3.51. Keeping more spectrum is not the same as coding it well. A codec that carries 15 kHz badly loses to one that carries 12 kHz cleanly, and no bandwidth number can see that difference. Note also that the AAC figures here come from ffmpeg's native encoder, which is not the encoder those tests used.
disagree_opus: At 128 kbps and above, graph B has almost nothing to separate the four codecs: bandwidth converges, sizes are within a few percent once you correct for Opus's VBR overshoot, and every decoder is fast enough. Graph A still separates them clearly, Opus at 4.65 against 4.40, 4.24 and 4.24 in 2014. The whole difference lives in how bits are allocated inside the bands both codecs keep, which is a psychoacoustic question and is invisible to every measurement on this page. This is the clearest case for why graph B cannot stand in for graph A: it is not that B is wrong, it is that B is silent.
disagree_encoder: Two MP3 files at 128 kbps have the same bitrate by definition, and measured here they would have near enough the same bandwidth as well. In the 2008 test LAME 3.98.2 scored 4.51 and l3enc scored 1.56, 2.95 grades apart. Every measurement on this page is blind to that, because every measurement here is a property of the bitstream's envelope rather than of the decisions inside it. It is also the reason the AAC numbers in graph B carry a warning: ffmpeg's native AAC encoder is the weak end of that same spread.
disagree_agree: Here the two halves point the same way and reinforce each other. Measured: at 32 kbps MP3 kept only 5.9 kHz of the spectrum and libvorbis refused to encode at all. Cited: in 2011 plain AAC-LC at 48 kbps scored 1.66 out of 5, which is what the test organisers chose as the deliberately broken reference. Below about 64 kbps the older formats are not making a trade, they are failing, and that is the gap Opus and HE-AAC were designed to fill.
claim_vorbis: The behaviour is real and it belongs to Opus. Opus contains two codecs: SILK, a speech coder derived from Skype's, and CELT, a transform coder for music, and RFC 6716 defines a hybrid mode that switches between and blends them by bitrate and content. That is why it survives at 32 kbps on a voice. Vorbis has nothing like it: it is a single MDCT transform codec, and on the speech tracks of the 2014 test it came last of four, 4.01 against Opus at 4.80 and even behind the MP3. Vorbis was excellent for its time and is genuinely royalty free, but Opus was written by the same community to replace it and does so at every bitrate. Treat Vorbis as legacy: keep decoding it, stop encoding it. Its one remaining edge is that some old Android and game engine pipelines take Vorbis and not Opus.
claim_lame: Confirmed, and the numbers are more extreme than the claim. Same format, same bitrate, same samples, 2008: LAME 3.98.2 4.51, l3enc from 1994 1.56. Nearly three grades of the five point scale, purely from the encoder. The settings worth typing are LAME's VBR modes rather than a bitrate: measured on this corpus -V0 cost 249 kbps, -V2 175 kbps and -V5 109 kbps. -V2 is the long standing HydrogenAudio recommendation and is transparent for most listeners on most material; -V0 is the archival end. -b 320 is worse than pointless: it costs 71 kbps more than -V0 measured here, and no listening test has ever shown it sounding better.
claim_aac: Largely right, and a defensible favourite. AAC has been second in every multiformat test since 2011 and it is the only modern codec with genuinely universal hardware reach. The caveat is about the numbers on this page rather than about AAC: they come from ffmpeg's native AAC encoder, which is the weakest of the widely used ones. The 2011 AAC test measured 0.69 grades between the best and worst encoders of this one format at one bitrate, and ffmpeg's was not even in that field. So treat every AAC figure in graph B as the pessimistic case, exactly as the images page treats stock libjpeg-turbo, and use qaac or fdk-aac in practice.
claim_heaac: Right in shape, too generous in the ratio, and slightly off in the premise. HE-AAC v1 is designed for roughly 32 to 64 kbps, and at 96 kbps a sensible encoder has already switched to plain AAC-LC, so the comparison you want is AAC-LC at 96 against MP3. In 2014 that was measured directly: Apple AAC at 104 kbps scored 4.40 and LAME at 136 kbps scored 4.24, so AAC was worth roughly 1.31 times the MP3 bitrate, not 2.6 times. Where the claim does hold is lower down: in 2007 HE-AAC at 64 kbps scored 3.74 while plain AAC-LC needed 96 kbps to reach 4.59, and MP3 at 64 kbps is not usable at all. A 250 kbps MP3 is LAME -V0, which HydrogenAudio describes as transparent; nothing at 96 kbps in any published test has reached that.
claim_spotify: True historically and no longer the whole picture. Spotify was built on Ogg Vorbis and still uses it for the numbered quality tiers in the desktop and mobile apps, but its own support page now describes the web player as AAC at 128 and 256 kbit/s, the top app tier as roughly 320 kbit/s, and Premium lossless as FLAC. YouTube's audio is Opus. Apple Music is AAC with ALAC for its lossless tier. So the current industry answer is: AAC where reach matters, Opus where the client is a browser, FLAC for lossless, and Vorbis only where it is already deployed.
claim_wma: Honest answer: it is dead, and it did not die because it was bad. In the 2006 test WMA Pro scored 4.70 at 128 kbps, statistically tied with AAC, Vorbis and LAME, and in 2007 at 64 kbps it beat Vorbis. It lost on ecosystem, not on coding: no browser decodes it, no phone plays it, no streaming service uses it, and Microsoft itself has moved on. There is no reason to encode WMA today and one reason to keep a decoder around, which is old Windows Media content you did not create.
claim_better: There is: Opus. It won the 2011 test at 64 kbps (4.00 against Apple HE-AAC at 3.82) and the 2014 test at 96 kbps (4.65 against Apple AAC at 4.40), it is royalty free, it is an IETF standard rather than a licensed one, it covers 6 kbps to 510 kbps in one format, and it handles speech and music in the same bitstream. Every browser decodes it and it is what YouTube serves. The catch is the one thing a listening test cannot measure: car head units, Bluetooth A2DP, DAB receivers, hi-fi streamers and older phones very often do not speak it. Use Opus for anything you control end to end. Use AAC for anything you hand to a stranger's hardware.
method_corpus: Corpus: music synthwave (30s, CC BY 3.0), music ambient (30s, CC BY 3.0), music orchestral (30s, CC BY 3.0), piano solo (30s, Public domain), percussion (15s, CC BY-SA 4.0), speech en (30s, CC BY-SA 4.0). All were fetched as FLAC from Wikimedia Commons by scripts/audio/make_corpus.py, trimmed and normalised to 48 kHz 16-bit stereo WAV, which is what every encoder was given. Two synthetic probes were added, a log sweep and pink noise with a tone comb, because real recordings do not have steady energy at every frequency and the bandwidth question needs a signal that does. The probes are excluded from every size and bitrate figure. 408 encodes were measured in total.
method_bandwidth: Effective bandwidth is measured against the source, not against an absolute level. Both signals get a Welch power spectrum, and the reported figure is the frequency above which the decoded spectrum has fallen more than 20 dB below the source's own spectrum, ignoring any band where the source itself is more than 70 dB down and so has nothing to discard. Defining it that way means a recording that simply has no 18 kHz content cannot be mistaken for a codec lowpass. On real music the test frequently cannot answer, because the material has no usable energy up there, which is exactly why the stationary probe is the signal plotted; the table view carries both readings and the number of clips each is based on.
